title: 95% Rule Strategy
name: 95% Rule Strategy
metaDescription: 95% rule strategy for Philadelphia 1031 exchange investors identifying more properties than the standard limits allow, with the closing discipline the rule demands.

sections.html: The 95% rule exists for the Philadelphia investor who wants to name ten rowhouse conversion units or a dozen suburban candidates on one identification list and cannot make the math work under the standard limits. It is the least forgiving of the identification rules, and most investors who reach for it underestimate what closing on nearly everything actually requires. A list this long is easy to draft on paper and far harder to carry through to closing without a coordinator tracking every candidate at once.

sections.heading: What The 95% Rule Actually Demands
sections.html: The 95% rule removes both the three-property count limit and the 200% value ceiling, letting an investor identify as many properties as they want, regardless of combined value. In exchange, the investor must acquire at least 95% of the total value of everything named on the list. There is no partial credit for closing on most of the list; falling short of the threshold by even a small margin can disqualify the exchange back to the properties actually acquired, and sometimes further. Investors sometimes assume the 95% figure is a target to aim for, when it functions instead as a strict pass-or-fail line measured after the fact, with no partial outcome recognized between passing and comfortably failing it, regardless of how close the final number lands to the line.

sections.heading: Why This Rule Shows Up In A Philadelphia Portfolio Strategy
sections.html: An investor consolidating several small rowhouse or twin-unit conversion properties into one identification, or naming a long list of suburban office and flex candidates to hedge against a competitive buyer pool, can run past both the three-property count and the 200% value cap quickly. The 95% rule becomes the only path forward for that kind of list, but it converts what looked like flexibility into a near-total closing obligation.

sections.heading: Building A List Under This Rule Without Overreaching
sections.html:
A list built for the 95% rule needs a different level of diligence than a standard shortlist, because nearly every property on it has to actually close.

  • Confirm financing is realistic for each and every property on the list, including the smaller ones
  • Verify use-and-occupancy timing on any conversion property well before it is added to the notice
  • Check recorded tax-abatement status on each candidate where the improvement value matters to the total
  • Limit the list to properties the investor is genuinely prepared to acquire, not aspirational candidates
  • Keep written valuation support current on every property, since the threshold is measured against value rather than count

Padding the list with long-shot candidates under this rule carries a different kind of risk than under the 200% rule, because nearly all of them have to close, and a single weak candidate can drag the whole list below the required threshold.

sections.heading: Where This Rule Meets Philadelphia's Closing Realities
sections.html: Closing on 95% of a long list means absorbing whatever delays surface across a mix of property types at once, and Philadelphia's mix runs wide: a Center City office estoppel, a Navy Yard industrial appraisal, and a rowhouse conversion's final inspection can all be moving on different timelines inside the same 180-day period. An investor using the 95% rule needs closing coordination that tracks every property on the list as if it were the only one, because falling short on even one can pull the whole exchange below the threshold.

sections.heading: When This Rule Is The Wrong Tool
sections.html: Most Philadelphia investors do better under the three-property or 200% rule, which leave room to walk away from a candidate that stalls. The 95% rule fits a narrower case: an investor with a specific, well-underwritten list of properties they intend to close on regardless of minor complications, and not a list built to keep options open while the search continues. Choosing this rule to gain flexibility on the front end, without the closing discipline to match on the back end, is how an exchange gets into trouble. A broker or coordinator who has worked through a 95% rule identification before can usually tell within a few conversations whether a given list is realistic or overreaching.

faqs.q: How is the 95% rule different from the 200% rule?
faqs.a: The 200% rule caps the combined value of everything identified. The 95% rule removes that cap entirely but requires the investor to actually acquire at least 95% of the total value named on the list.

faqs.q: What happens if an investor closes on only 90% of the identified value?
faqs.a: Falling short of the 95% threshold can disqualify the exchange treatment for the properties that were not acquired, and in some cases can put the entire exchange at risk depending on how the shortfall arose.

faqs.q: Why would a Philadelphia investor choose this rule over the three-property rule?
faqs.a: It fits an investor consolidating many smaller properties, such as several rowhouse conversion units, into one identification where the count or combined value would otherwise exceed the standard limits.

faqs.q: Does the 95% rule require closing on every single identified property?
faqs.a: No, but it requires closing on enough of them to reach 95% of the total identified value, which in practice usually means closing on nearly all of them unless one is a very small share of the list.

faqs.q: Is the 95% rule riskier than the other identification rules?
faqs.a: Yes, because it removes the option to let a struggling candidate fall away without consequence. It works best for investors with high confidence in closing every property on the list.
